title: When to call a geriatric care manager, and what they actually do
dek: A care manager is a professional guide for families facing aging, illness or a sudden crisis. Here is what they do, what to ask, and how to find a good one in New Jersey.
keyFacts: Geriatric care managers are also called aging life care professionals.
Most are licensed social workers or nurses with years of experience in aging.
They assess, plan, coordinate care, advocate with doctors and keep distant family informed.
Medicare does not pay for private care management. AARP reports rates of about $150 to $300 an hour.
The Aging Life Care Association lists members by location.
body:
Most families never plan to need help. Then Mom falls, Dad gets a new diagnosis, or the person who was quietly managing everything can't anymore. Suddenly you are juggling doctors, insurance, home care agencies and siblings in three time zones.

That is the moment a geriatric care manager earns their fee. Think of one as a professional guide who knows the local system, has seen your situation many times before, and works for your family rather than for a hospital or an agency.

What does a care manager do?

A good care manager starts with a full assessment. They visit your parent at home, talk with the family and review medications, health history, safety, finances and daily routines. From there they write a care plan with short and long term goals.

After that, the work depends on what your family needs. Common tasks include:

  • Finding, screening and overseeing home care aides
  • Going to medical appointments and making sure everyone leaves with the same plan
  • Advocating with doctors, hospitals and rehab centers
  • Helping a family compare assisted living, memory care or nursing homes
  • Sorting out paperwork, bills and benefit applications
  • Stepping in during a crisis, such as a hospital discharge on a Friday afternoon
  • Keeping adult children who live far away up to date
  • Helping siblings who disagree reach a plan everyone can live with
A care manager works for your family, not for the hospital or the agency.

How is care management different from home care?

Families mix these up all the time, and the difference matters when you are deciding what to pay for.

Home care is hands-on help. An aide or companion comes to the house to help with bathing, dressing, meals, light housekeeping or simply keeping someone company. A home health agency may also send nurses or therapists after a hospital stay.

Care management is planning and coordination. The care manager figures out what kind of help your parent really needs, finds it, checks that it is working and adjusts the plan when things change. They do not usually give the hands-on care themselves. AARP describes them as project managers for care.

That matters for your budget. A care manager may tell you that a few hours of a companion each week is enough, where you assumed you needed a nurse. Or they may spot that a parent needs more help than the family realized.

It also matters for insurance. Medicare's home health benefit covers part-time skilled care, such as nursing or therapy, for people who are homebound and whose doctor orders it. It does not cover 24-hour care at home, and it does not cover help with bathing or dressing when that is the only care someone needs. Neither Medicare nor Medicaid typically pays for a private care manager.

Who becomes a care manager?

Most care managers are licensed clinical social workers or registered nurses who have spent years working with older adults. Others come from counseling or gerontology. The field's professional group is the Aging Life Care Association, which sets education, experience and certification requirements for members and has a code of ethics and standards of practice.

Some social workers also hold the C-ASWCM credential, which stands for Certified Advanced Social Work Case Manager. It is issued by the National Association of Social Workers and requires a master's degree in social work, a state license at the master's level (or a passing score on the national exam) and at least two years of supervised case management experience.

Credentials matter because this person may be in the room for some of the hardest decisions your family makes. Ask about licensing, certification and how many years they have worked with older adults in your county.

What does the first assessment cover?

The assessment is the foundation for everything else. AARP notes that it often takes four to six hours, sometimes spread over more than one visit, and is usually billed once. Seeing your parent at home tells a care manager things a phone call never will, such as loose rugs, an empty refrigerator or a stack of unopened mail.

The Aging Life Care Association describes eight areas of expertise its members bring. A thorough assessment usually touches all of them:

  • Health and disability. Diagnoses, medications, memory, mobility, falls and how well daily tasks are going.
  • Financial. Whether bills are paid, what care the family can afford and which benefits might help.
  • Housing. Whether the home is safe now and whether it will work in a year or two.
  • Families. Who is helping, who lives far away, and where the family agrees or disagrees.
  • Local resources. Which agencies, day programs, transportation and county services fit your parent's situation.
  • Advocacy. Your parent's own wishes, and how to make sure doctors and facilities hear them.
  • Legal. Whether a power of attorney and an advance directive exist, and when to bring in an elder law attorney.
  • Crisis intervention. A plan for the next fall, hospital stay or sudden change.

At the end, you should receive a written care plan with clear recommendations, what each one is likely to cost and who will do what.

What might the first month look like?

Every family is different, but here is a hypothetical example. Say your father lives alone in Bloomfield, recently fell, and you live in Chicago.

  1. Week one: the first call and the visit. You describe what is happening and agree on fees in writing. The care manager visits your father at home, meets a local relative and reviews his medications and papers.
  2. Week two: the care plan. You get a written plan. It might suggest grab bars, a medication review with his doctor, a few hours of help each week and a call to the county office on aging about meals or rides.
  3. Week three: putting help in place. The care manager helps interview home care agencies, sets up the first shifts and goes with your father to a doctor appointment so everyone hears the same plan.
  4. Week four: checking in. They visit again to see whether the aide is a good fit and whether your father is safer and happier. You get an update by phone or email, and the plan is adjusted.

After that, many families keep the care manager on call for check-ins, crises and big decisions, and pay only for the time used.

When is it time to call one?

You don't need to wait for an emergency. These are common moments when families reach out:

  • A parent was just discharged from the hospital and nobody is sure what happens next
  • You live out of state and can't be there for appointments
  • Memory problems are starting to affect bills, driving or medications
  • Siblings disagree about whether a parent should move
  • A home care aide isn't working out and you don't know where to turn
  • You suspect someone is taking advantage of a parent financially
  • You are the main caregiver and you are running out of steam
Try the free route first, too

Your county office on aging can screen for programs, meals and rides at no cost. Call 1-877-222-3737. Care management is also built into some public programs, including Medicaid's Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) and the state's JACC program, for people who qualify. Many families use both: the county for public programs, and a private care manager for hands-on coordination.

What does it cost?

Private care management is usually paid by the hour, and Medicare does not cover it. AARP reports hourly rates of roughly $150 to $300, depending on the region. Many care managers charge separately for the first assessment and then bill for ongoing work as needed. Some also bill for travel time and mileage.

A few ways the cost may be offset: some long-term care insurance policies reimburse part of it, and some employers' employee assistance programs cover a consultation. Check the policy or call your human resources office before you start.

Ask for fees in writing before the first visit. A clear care manager will tell you what the assessment costs, how they bill for phone calls and travel, and how they will keep you updated.

Questions to ask before you hire

  1. Are you licensed, and are you a member of the Aging Life Care Association?
  2. How long have you worked with older adults in this area?
  3. Who covers for you on nights, weekends and vacations?
  4. How do you communicate with family members, and how often?
  5. Do you receive referral fees from any agency or facility you recommend? (The answer should be no.)
  6. Can you share references from families or local professionals?

It also helps to have a few papers ready. Ask your parent to sign the doctor's office permission forms so the care manager and family can talk with the medical team. If your parent has a durable power of attorney or an advance directive, bring copies. Our guide to estate planning in New Jersey explains these documents.

A care management practice we know well

Connections Care Management is a care management practice with offices in Montclair, New Jersey and Suffern, New York. It serves Bergen, Essex, Passaic, Union, Hudson, Morris and Middlesex counties in New Jersey, plus Rockland County in New York.

The practice is led by Lisa Kolton, LCSW, C-ASWCM, and Kim Hamilton, LCSW, C-ASWCM. Both are licensed clinical social workers with more than 25 years of experience with older adults and their families, and both hold the C-ASWCM care management credential. Their services include assessments and care plans, going to medical appointments, overseeing home care, help choosing senior housing, benefit applications, crisis help and protection from financial exploitation.

Families can reach Lisa Kolton at 973-747-5571 or Kim Hamilton at 845-480-1561, or learn more at caremanagementconnect.net.

Full disclosure: Lisa Kolton is the mother of this site's publisher. We mention her practice because we know firsthand the care she gives families, and we encourage you to ask any care manager the questions above.

How to find other care managers

The Aging Life Care Association has a search tool that lists members by ZIP code and distance. Your doctor, a hospital social worker or an elder law attorney can also suggest names. Speak with two or three before choosing, and pick the one who listens best.

Just starting to worry about a parent? Our guide to talking with a parent about getting help covers the first steps, and help for family caregivers lists New Jersey's respite programs.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for a geriatric care manager?
faq.a: No. Private care management is not covered by Medicare. Some long-term care insurance policies reimburse part of the cost, so check your policy.

faq.q: How much does a geriatric care manager cost?
faq.a: AARP reports hourly rates of roughly $150 to $300, depending on the region. The first assessment often takes four to six hours and is usually billed once, so ask for all fees in writing.

faq.q: Is a care manager the same as a home health aide?
faq.a: No. An aide provides hands-on care such as bathing and meals. A care manager is a licensed professional who assesses, plans and coordinates all of the care, including aides.

faq.q: What happens at a care manager's first assessment?
faq.a: The care manager visits your parent at home and reviews health, medications, safety, finances, family support and legal papers. You then get a written care plan with recommendations and likely costs.

faq.q: Can a care manager help if I live out of state?
faq.a: Yes. Keeping long-distance family informed is one of the most common reasons people hire one.

faq.q: Is there a free alternative?
faq.a: Your county office on aging offers free screening and referrals. Call 1-877-222-3737 to reach yours. People who qualify for MLTSS or JACC also get care management through those programs.

title: Home Happenings: lessons and activities that come to your living room
dek: A New Jersey company that sends checked local pros to older adults' homes to teach music, art, yoga, cooking, games, tech and more, starting in Essex and Passaic counties.
keyFacts: Home Happenings is launching in Essex and Passaic counties, in towns from Montclair and West Orange to Clifton and Woodland Park.
Activities: music, art, personal training, yoga, gardening, board and card games, chess, cooking, tech help and personal storytelling.
Pros set their own rates, starting at $50 an hour, for sessions of 1, 1.5 or 2 hours. There is no membership.
Every pro passes a criminal background check, a national sex offender registry check and an interview before they are listed.
Questions: (201) 431-5135 or contact@homehappenings.com
body:
For a lot of older adults, the hard part of staying active isn't motivation. It's getting there. The card game moved across town, driving at night got harder, or a knee surgery turned into months of not painting. The interest never went away. The easy way to keep doing it did.

Home Happenings flips that around. Instead of going to the lesson, the lesson comes to you.

What is Home Happenings?

Home Happenings is a New Jersey company that matches older adults, and the families who book for them, with local pros who come to the house to teach a lesson or lead an activity. Sessions happen at the kitchen table, in the living room or out in the garden, on your schedule and at your pace.

A retired engineer can finally learn piano. A grandmother can start watercolors at home. Four friends can set up a weekly game night without anyone driving after dark.

Where it works

Home Happenings is starting in Essex and Passaic counties, getting to know each pro one by one. Towns include Bloomfield, Caldwell, Cedar Grove, Clifton, Essex Fells, Fairfield, Glen Ridge, Little Falls, Livingston, Maplewood, Millburn, Montclair, North Caldwell, Nutley, Roseland, Short Hills, South Orange, Verona, West Caldwell, West Orange and Woodland Park. You can search by ZIP code to see which pros can come to you.

What can you book?

  • Music lessons: piano, guitar, voice and more
  • Art lessons: painting, drawing and other crafts
  • Personal training: strength and balance work, at a comfortable pace
  • Yoga: including gentle and chair yoga
  • Gardening: help planning, planting and tending a garden or a few pots
  • Board and card games: learn a new game or get a regular table going
  • Chess: lessons for beginners and returning players
  • Cooking lessons: new recipes or old favorites, in your own kitchen
  • Tech help: patient help with phones, tablets, video calls and email
  • Personal storytelling: a guide helps you tell your life stories so your family can keep them

You can also filter pros by language, including Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, Russian, Hebrew, Yiddish, Polish, Korean, Mandarin, Hindi, Gujarati, Tagalog, Haitian Creole, French and Arabic.

Keep doing what you love, without leaving home to do it.

How it works

  1. Look. Browse local pros by town, activity or ZIP code, read their profiles and message anyone with questions.
  2. Book. Pick a session of 1, 1.5 or 2 hours and an open time. Book once, four weeks at the same time, or every week until you cancel.
  3. Enjoy. Your pro comes to the house and teaches. Book again whenever you like, or keep the same pro every week.

What it costs

Each pro sets their own hourly rate, starting at $50. Each session adds a 9% service fee, and there is one $2.50 booking fee per checkout. You pay when you book, and there is no membership.

Travel within 10 miles is free. Some pros travel up to 30 miles, and for homes more than 10 miles away there is a $30 travel fee per session, shown before you book. Cancelling more than 24 hours ahead is free, apart from the service fee.

How pros are checked

Letting someone into your home is a big deal. Before a pro is listed, they pass five checks: an online search, a real conversation with the Home Happenings team, a signed provider agreement, a criminal background check and a national sex offender registry check. Every booked session is also covered by the company's general liability insurance, and your address stays private until a session is confirmed.

Booking for a parent

Adult children can create the account, say who the sessions are for and where they live, and book from anywhere. You get the booking emails and can message the pro. Many families book the first session themselves so it is on the calendar, then let Mom or Dad take it from there.

Gift cards are available too, starting at $50. They never expire, carry no fees and work with any pro and any activity.

For senior communities

Independent and assisted living communities, 55+ communities and community programs can book pros to teach group classes on site. A community fills out a short form and the team reaches out within one business day to set up the first classes.

Making the first session a good one

  • Start with something familiar. An old love, like the piano someone played as a teenager or the card game they used to host, is often an easier first step than something brand new.
  • Pick a time of day that works. Many people have more energy in the morning or early afternoon. Avoid squeezing a session between doctor visits.
  • Set up the space. A clear table, a comfortable chair and good light go a long way, whether it is watercolors, cards or a tablet.
  • Share a little background. Let the pro know anything that helps them teach well, such as hearing that is better on one side or a hand that tires quickly.
  • Give it a few weeks. The real payoff of a weekly session is the rhythm. Something to look forward to on Tuesday afternoon can change how the whole week feels.

Who it's for

Home Happenings is built for older adults living at home or in senior communities, and for the spouses, adult children, grandchildren and friends who want someone they love to have something to look forward to. Anyone who wants a lesson at home can book, at any age.

  • Someone who has stopped driving at night, or at all, and misses the classes and clubs that used to fill the calendar.
  • A person getting back on their feet after an illness or a hospital stay who is not ready for a busy class across town.
  • A couple or a group of neighbors who would rather learn something together in someone's living room.
  • A family caregiver who would welcome an hour when a parent is happily busy with someone else.
  • Adult children who live far away and want to give a parent something to enjoy, not another errand to manage.

Home Happenings is not home care. Pros teach or lead activities, and they do not provide medical services or personal care. If a parent needs help with bathing, meals or medications, our guide to talking with a parent about getting help covers where to start.

Learn more

Visit homehappenings.com, call 201-431-5135 or email contact@homehappenings.com. You can also follow along on Instagram.

Full disclosure: Home Happenings is run by the publisher of Seniors of NJ.

title: When a parent stops driving in NJ: rides, ID and staying connected
dek: Signs it may be time, how to start the talk, the non-driver ID, every county paratransit number, NJ Transit options and how to keep your mom or dad active and social without the car.
keyFacts: Every NJ county runs a paratransit service for older residents. Hours and fees vary, so call.
NJ MVC non-driver ID: residents 14+, $24, in person by appointment, 6 Points of ID.
NJ Transit reduced fares start at 62. The reduced fare card cannot be used on Access Link.
Access Link (ADA paratransit): 973-491-4224, option 1 for eligibility.
NJTIP at Rutgers teaches older adults to ride transit: 848-932-4499.
body:
For most people in New Jersey, the car is how life happens. It gets you to the doctor, the store, the senior center, Sunday services and the diner where your friends meet. So when a parent stops driving, the worry is bigger than rides.

In our October 2026 conversations with North Jersey instructors, families and care professionals, one person put the worry plainly: "If I stop driving, then what am I going to do?" People also told us that many older adults give up the things they love only because they can no longer get there. This guide is about making sure that does not happen to your mom or dad.

For help with the earlier stage, when a parent is still driving and you want to keep them safe behind the wheel, see our guide to driving later in life in New Jersey.

What are the signs it may be time to stop driving?

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) says decisions about driving should never be based on age alone. Most older drivers have a lifetime of experience. What matters is how changes in vision, strength, reflexes and attention affect driving.

NHTSA's guide, developed with AARP and the USAA Educational Foundation, lists signs worth taking seriously:

  • Trouble reading street signs or seeing lane lines, curbs and pedestrians, especially at dusk or night.
  • Trouble turning to look over a shoulder, or moving a foot from gas to brake.
  • Feeling overwhelmed at busy intersections, or finding gaps in traffic hard to judge.
  • Getting lost on routes that used to be familiar.
  • Several moving violations, near misses or crashes in the last three years.
  • A warning from a police officer, even without a ticket.
  • Medicines that cause sleepiness, or episodes of dizziness or blacking out.
  • A doctor advising them to limit or stop driving.
  • A friend or family member expressing concern.

Look for patterns over several weeks. Everyone has a bad day. Ride along a few times on different roads and at different times of day. Look at the car for new dents and scrapes.

Not sure? Get a professional opinion

A certified driver rehabilitation specialist can test driving skills and recommend changes, limits or equipment. New Jersey's Division of Disability Services keeps a list of specialists serving NJ residents on its transportation page. The doctor is also a good first call.

How do you start the conversation?

NHTSA notes that most families delay this talk until driving already feels dangerous, and then it becomes tense. Starting earlier is kinder. It suggests three steps: collect information, develop a plan, and follow through.

  1. Gather facts first. Note what you have seen, with dates. "You scraped the garage twice this month" lands better than "you're a bad driver now."
  2. Choose the right messenger. Some parents listen to a doctor or a trusted friend more easily than to their children.
  3. Lead with what stays the same. Start with the plan for keeping their life full. "You'll still get to cards every Tuesday. Here's how."
  4. Consider steps in between. Daytime only, no highways, familiar routes only. NHTSA suggests these as ways to stay safe longer.
  5. Expect more than one talk. Grief and anger are normal. Giving up the keys is a real loss.
  6. Follow through. Have the rides lined up before the last drive. A plan on paper is not the same as a ride that shows up.

If the conversation is part of a bigger worry about living alone, our guides to the first conversation about care and a parent living alone can help.

What ID does your parent use without a driver's license?

A photo ID is still needed for the bank, the pharmacy and travel. The New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission (MVC) issues a non-driver photo ID to residents 14 and older.

  • The first card must be obtained in person by appointment at an MVC Licensing Center.
  • Bring the application (Form BA-208) and documents that meet the 6 Points of ID requirement.
  • The fee is $24. The card is mailed.
  • Residents with a disability can get a non-driver ID with a physician's certification. The MVC lists an initial fee of $6 and no renewal fee.

Our non-driver ID guide explains the documents and what to expect at the appointment.

How can your parent get around New Jersey without a car?

Options vary a lot by town. Most families end up using several, depending on the trip.

County paratransit

The NJ Department of Human Services says each of New Jersey's 21 counties provides a paratransit service for older residents and people with disabilities. Hours, reservation rules, trip types and fees vary, so call. These are the numbers the state lists:

NJ Transit Access Link

Access Link is NJ Transit's paratransit service for people with disabilities who cannot use local buses or light rail. It runs in the same areas and hours as local bus service. It is shared-ride and curb-to-curb, and it is not free. Riders need an eligibility interview first. Call 973-491-4224 and choose option 1. NJ Transit notes the reduced fare card cannot be used on Access Link.

Reduced fares on buses and trains

NJ Transit offers reduced fares to riders 62 and older. The state says riders 65 and older can show a Reduced Fare ID or Medicare card, and riders 62 to 64 may be asked for ID with their date of birth. See our reduced fare guide.

If your parent has never ridden a bus, the New Jersey Travel Independence Program (NJTIP) at Rutgers teaches older adults and people with disabilities to use public transit. The state says the only cost during training is the rider's own fares. Call 848-932-4499.

Town senior buses

Many towns and senior centers run their own shuttles for shopping, meals and programs. Call your town hall or senior center and ask. Our county pages, such as senior centers in Essex County, list local contacts.

Rideshare, taxis and phone-based ride services

Rideshare apps work well for some older adults, especially if a family member sets up the account and tracks rides. Some services let you book a rideshare or car by phone, with no smartphone needed. Before you sign up, ask who the drivers are, how they are screened, how you are billed and what happens if a ride does not show.

Home care staff told us most aides do not drive clients, so do not assume a home care agency will solve transportation. Ask directly. If your parent has NJ FamilyCare, the state lists ModivCare for non-emergency medical rides at 1-866-527-9933, with requests two days ahead.

How do you keep your parent active and social without the car?

Rides solve part of the problem. The rest is making sure there are still good reasons to get dressed in the morning.

  • Keep the anchors. List the three or four things your parent loves most and set up a ride for each, every week, at the same time.
  • Ask friends. Many people are glad to share a ride to church or cards. Offer gas money or a meal to make it easy to say yes.
  • Bring activities home. When getting out is hard, the activity can come to the house. Invite the card group over, or hire a private instructor for art, music or exercise. In our October 2026 conversations, private instructors in North Jersey said they generally charge about $60 to $150 an hour.
  • Go online for some things. Video calls, online classes and phone-in programs fill gaps. See staying connected and tech help for seniors.
  • Get groceries and meals delivered. That saves the rides for the things that matter. See Meals on Wheels.
Rides matter. Something to look forward to every week matters more.

Before anyone new comes into your parent's home or drives them, check references, ask about background checks and insurance, and keep money matters in the family. Our guide to vetting in-home help and our scams guide cover what to watch for.

What should families do in the first month?

  1. Write down every regular trip. Doctor, pharmacy, groceries, hair, worship, friends, activities.
  2. Match each trip to a ride. County paratransit, a town shuttle, a friend, family, rideshare or delivery.
  3. Make a ride sheet. Phone numbers, booking rules and how far ahead to call, posted by the phone.
  4. Get the non-driver ID. Do it before the license expires or is surrendered.
  5. Decide about the car. Selling it can cover a lot of rides. Insurance, gas, repairs and parking add up.
  6. Check in often. Ask what they missed this week, not just whether the rides worked.

If your parent seems withdrawn or sad, mention it to the doctor. Losing the car can feel like losing independence. With a good plan, it does not have to mean losing a full life.

faq.q: How do I tell my dad he needs to stop driving?
faq.a: Gather specific examples first, pick the messenger he trusts most (sometimes his doctor), and lead with the plan for keeping his life full. Consider steps in between, like daytime driving only. Expect more than one conversation, and have rides set up before the last drive.

faq.q: Can a doctor or specialist test whether my parent is safe to drive?
faq.a: Yes. A certified driver rehabilitation specialist can evaluate driving skills and recommend limits or equipment. The NJ Division of Disability Services lists specialists serving NJ residents. Start by talking with your parent's doctor.

faq.q: What ID can my mom use if she gives up her license?
faq.a: The NJ Motor Vehicle Commission issues a non-driver photo ID. The first one requires an in-person appointment at a Licensing Center, Form BA-208, 6 Points of ID and a $24 fee. The card is mailed.

faq.q: Is there free transportation for seniors in New Jersey?
faq.a: Each county runs paratransit for older residents and people with disabilities, and many towns run senior shuttles. Fees vary by county and trip, so call your county number. NJ Transit offers reduced fares from age 62. Access Link charges a fare.

faq.q: How do I keep my parent from getting isolated after they stop driving?
faq.a: Keep their favorite weekly activities and set up a regular ride for each. Ask friends to share rides, bring some activities into the home, and use video calls and phone-in programs to fill gaps. Check in about what they missed, not only about rides.

body:
Every family has stories that live in one person's head. How your parents met. What the old neighborhood in Newark or Paterson or Camden was like. The job your dad took right out of the Army. The recipe your mom never wrote down.

A life story project gets those stories onto paper or a recording while there is still time to ask. It can be a printed book, a set of audio interviews, a video or a simple binder of typed pages. This guide covers how it works, what it costs to hire help, how to do it yourself, where New Jersey libraries offer memoir programs, and how to approach it when a parent has memory loss.

What is a life story or memoir project?

At its simplest, someone asks good questions and someone else listens and records. The answers become a keepsake for children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

Common forms include:

  • A written memoir or life story book, often with family photos.
  • Recorded interviews, audio or video, kept as files and sometimes edited into a short film.
  • A legacy letter, a few pages about values, lessons and hopes for the family.
  • A recipe and story book, where each dish comes with the memory behind it.
  • A photo history, captioned in your parent's own words.

Older adults often get more out of it than the family expects. In our October 2026 conversations with North Jersey instructors, families and care professionals, writers who do this work called it therapeutic and restorative. Looking back over a whole life can bring perspective, pride and sometimes peace. It is also a reason to spend real time together.

How does working with a personal historian or memoir writer work?

Some families hire a writer to interview their parent and turn the conversations into a finished book. Here is what we heard from writers in our October 2026 conversations:

QuestionWhat writers told us
How many sessions?About 4 to 7. Seven is ideal, four is a minimum.
How long is each session?Usually 60 to 90 minutes.
What does it cost?Often about $100 a session, sometimes more for a video version.
What do you end up with?Usually a book.

These are typical figures from a small group of North Jersey writers, not set prices. Always get a written quote that says what is included: how many sessions, transcription, editing, photos, design, printing and how many copies.

Questions to ask before you hire someone

  • Can I see samples of finished books or recordings?
  • Can you give me two references from families you worked with?
  • Who owns the recordings and the finished text? Will we get the raw audio files?
  • How do you keep private stories private? Will anything be shared or posted?
  • Can family members sit in on sessions?
  • How do payments work? Paying per session or in stages is safer than paying everything up front.

The writer will be in your parent's home and will hear personal stories, sometimes about money, family conflict or health. Trust matters. Ask about background checks and insurance, be there for the first session, and make sure your parent never shares bank details, account numbers or checks with anyone working on the project. Our guide to vetting in-home help has a full checklist.

Can you do it yourself?

Yes, and many families do. You need curiosity, a phone that records and a few hours spread over several weeks.

Start with good questions

Open-ended questions work best. A few to start:

  • What is your earliest memory?
  • Tell me about the house you grew up in. What did it smell like? Who lived there?
  • What did your parents do for work?
  • How did you meet Mom (or Dad)? What was your first date?
  • What was your first job? What did you buy with your first paycheck?
  • What was the hardest year of your life, and how did you get through it?
  • What are you proudest of?
  • What has changed most in your town since you were young?
  • What do you want your grandchildren to know about you?

Pick one theme per session: childhood, work, love and marriage, raising a family, faith, places you lived. That keeps it from feeling like an exam.

The StoryCorps App

StoryCorps offers a free mobile app that guides you through preparing questions, recording a conversation on your phone and uploading the audio. StoryCorps says recordings can be archived with the Library of Congress and the StoryCorps Archive. Before uploading, talk with your parent about whether they want their story in a public archive or kept in the family.

The Veterans History Project

If your parent served in the military, the Library of Congress Veterans History Project collects oral history interviews and original materials, like letters and photos, from U.S. veterans. Family members and friends can conduct the interview. The project's website has step-by-step guidelines. Call 202-707-4916 with questions. See also our guide to veterans benefits in New Jersey.

How do you record a good interview at home?

  1. Find a quiet room. Turn off the TV and radio. Soft furniture and rugs cut echo.
  2. Test the recording. Record 30 seconds and play it back. Put the phone close to your parent, on a book or stand, not in your hand.
  3. Keep sessions short. An hour is plenty for most people. Stop while it is still fun.
  4. Say the date and names at the start. "It's November 2, and I'm talking with my mother about growing up in Bayonne."
  5. Bring props. Old photos, a yearbook, a recipe card or a medal can unlock stories that questions cannot.
  6. Listen more than you talk. Ask "what happened next?" and "how did that feel?" Let silences sit.
  7. Back up the files. Save copies in two places the same day, and label them clearly.
The best question is often the simplest one: "Tell me more about that."

If your parent has hearing loss, sit facing them in good light and speak clearly. Our hearing aids guide covers hearing help and programs in New Jersey.

Where can older adults learn memoir writing in New Jersey?

Some older adults would rather write their own story. New Jersey public libraries run memoir groups and workshops, often free or low cost. Two ongoing examples we confirmed on library calendars:

  • Oradell Public Library (Bergen County) hosts a Memoir and Creative Writing Workshop on the second Wednesday of the month, 1 to 2:30 p.m. Email oradcirc@bccls.org or call 201-262-2613.
  • Plainfield Public Library (Union County) runs a monthly Memoir Writing Club on the second Thursday, 10:30 a.m. to noon, where members write about a topic each month. Recent meetings have been hybrid or on Zoom only, so ask which format applies.

Schedules change, so call ahead. Many other libraries run memoir workshops from time to time, so check your own library's events calendar too. Our guides to learning something new and staying connected list more classes, and your county office on aging can point you to programs at senior centers. Call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737.

How do you give a life story as a gift?

Many older adults are careful with money and do not want it spent on them. In our conversations, families said framing a project as a gift helps. A memoir works well for a milestone birthday, an anniversary, Mother's Day, Father's Day or the holidays.

  • Give a card that explains the plan, with the first session date already set.
  • Split the cost among siblings so it feels like a family gift.
  • Plan a small reading or showing when it is done. Hearing grandchildren read the stories aloud can mean as much as the book.
  • Order extra copies for siblings, cousins and grandchildren.

Our gift ideas for older parents has more ideas.

What if your parent has memory loss?

A life story project can still work, and it can be a comfort. It takes a gentler approach.

  • Start sooner. If there is an early diagnosis, begin now while long-term memories are strongest.
  • Use photos and music. Care professionals told us music often reaches people with dementia. Play songs from their young adult years and ask what they remember.
  • Keep it short. A therapy practice we spoke with said one hour on a single activity is hard for many people with dementia. Try 15 to 20 minutes, and switch between talking, photos and music.
  • Do not correct. If a date or name is wrong, let it go. The feeling of the story matters more than the facts.
  • Include other voices. Siblings, old friends and neighbors can fill in parts of the story.
  • Watch for distress. Some memories bring up grief. Change the subject gently if a topic upsets them.

A simple "memory book" with large photos and short captions can also help day to day, for family and for paid caregivers who are getting to know your parent. See activities for dementia, music and dementia and dementia support in NJ.

However you do it, start with one conversation. The stories are there. Someone just has to ask.

faq.q: How do I get my mom's life story written down before it's too late?
faq.a: Start with one recorded conversation this month. Use a phone, a quiet room and one theme, like childhood or how she met your father. If you want a finished book, a personal historian can interview her over several sessions and write it for you.

faq.q: How much does it cost to hire someone to write a parent's memoir?
faq.a: North Jersey writers we spoke with in October 2026 often charged about $100 a session, over about 4 to 7 sessions of 60 to 90 minutes, sometimes more for video. Get a written quote that lists editing, photos, printing and number of copies.

faq.q: Is there a free way to record a parent's stories?
faq.a: Yes. The free StoryCorps App helps you prepare questions, record on your phone and upload the conversation if you choose. Veterans can also share their story with the Library of Congress Veterans History Project.

faq.q: Can you do a life story project with someone who has dementia?
faq.a: Often yes. Keep sessions short, use photos and familiar music, do not correct mistakes, and invite other family members to fill in details. Starting soon after a diagnosis, while long-term memories are strongest, helps.

faq.q: Do NJ libraries have memoir writing classes for seniors?
faq.a: Some do. Oradell Public Library hosts a monthly memoir and creative writing workshop, and Plainfield Public Library runs a monthly memoir club that has met in person and on Zoom. Check your own library's calendar too.

body:
Bergen County has one of the strongest senior center networks in New Jersey. The county itself runs ten senior activity centers, each with a weekday lunch, and many towns run their own on top of that. If you live here and you are 60 or older, there is very likely a place within a short ride where you can eat lunch with other people, take an exercise class and find something to look forward to every week.

This guide lists the centers we could confirm on official county and town pages, explains how lunch and rides work, and gives a few tips for a first visit. It is written for older adults and for the sons, daughters and spouses who often make the first call.

What do Bergen County senior centers offer, and who can go?

The county's ten centers are run by the Bergen County Division of Senior Services. Their monthly calendars say activities and programs are free for Bergen County residents 60 and over. They are open Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., and closed on county holidays.

A typical week mixes exercise and social time. The November 2026 calendar at the Bergenfield center, for example, lists qigong and tai chi, yoga, Zumba, cardio, ceramics, dance classes, Scrabble, Rummikub and several rounds of bingo, plus a continental breakfast each morning. Garfield adds a billiards room and a computer room. Workshops on brain health, medications and life changes come up often.

Town-run centers set their own rules. Paramus and Mahwah list their centers for residents 62 and over. Ramsey's is free for people 60 and older who live in or own property in town. Westwood's ForeverYoung program welcomes adults 55 and up, and the Southeast Senior Center for Independent Living in Englewood lists free membership from age 57. The 55 Kip Center in Rutherford is a nonprofit with a small yearly membership fee ($10 for Rutherford residents, $15 for others).

If your parent says "I'm not a senior center person," start with one class they would enjoy anywhere, like tai chi or ceramics.

Ridgewood's Community Center is being renovated this fall, so its senior classes have moved to Village Hall and the Stable for now. For any town not listed, see our Bergen County page or call the Division of Senior Services at 201-336-7400.

How does lunch work at the county centers?

Every county center serves a hot lunch on weekdays through the county's Senior Lunch program. You must be 60 or older, or the spouse of a participant. The meal is free, with a suggested donation of $1.25. Donations are voluntary and confidential, and nobody is turned away for not giving.

You do need a reservation. The county says to book at least one day ahead, and the center calendars ask you to reserve by 11:30 a.m. the day before. Lunch is served at 11:30 a.m. The menu is printed on each center's monthly calendar, so you can see ahead of time whether it is chicken Florentine or meatloaf day.

If getting out is not realistic right now, Bergen County Meals on Wheels delivers a midday meal on weekdays to homebound residents in many towns. Call 201-336-7420. Our Meals on Wheels guide explains how the assessment works.

How can you get to a center without driving?

Bergen County's Division of Community Transportation gives rides to seniors, frail residents and people with disabilities who live in the county. The county says Community Transportation provides rides to and from all ten centers, and also to medical visits, physical therapy, shopping and other senior services. Call 201-368-5955 and press 1 for dispatch to ask about getting on a route.

Some towns run their own senior buses too. Ask your borough or township recreation office. For longer trips, our guide to NJ Transit reduced fares covers bus and train discounts for riders 62 and over.

In our October 2026 conversations with North Jersey instructors, families and care professionals, people told us again and again that many older adults stop doing what they love only because they can no longer get there. A standing ride to the center can fix that. If your parent has just stopped driving, our guide on what to do when a parent stops driving has more ideas.

What if your town has no senior center?

You are not stuck. The county centers are open to every Bergen County resident 60 and older, no matter which town you live in. Wyckoff residents, for instance, are near the Northwest center in Midland Park.

  • Call the county first. The Division of Senior Services at 201-336-7400 can tell you which center is closest and whether Community Transportation covers your street.
  • Check your library. Many Bergen libraries run free talks, book clubs and tech help. See our guide to staying connected.
  • Ask about clubs. Many towns have a seniors club that meets once or twice a month even without a full center.

What helps on a first visit?

  1. Call ahead. Ask what is on the calendar that day and reserve lunch by the deadline.
  2. Bring ID and proof of address. County centers serve county residents, and some town centers ask for proof of residency and age to sign up.
  3. Pick one activity. Arriving for a specific class is easier than walking into a room cold.
  4. Go together the first time. Adult children can sit in for the first hour, then step out. Staff are used to this.
  5. Try it three times. The first visit can feel awkward. By the third, people start saving you a seat.

A note for families: you can call a center on your parent's behalf, ask about the schedule and even request a calendar by mail. If memory loss makes a group setting hard, ask the county about adult day programs instead, or browse care help near you. Our guide on a parent living alone covers other ways to keep them connected.

faq.q: Do I have to live in the town where the senior center is?
faq.a: Not for the ten county-run centers. Any Bergen County resident 60 or older can use them. Town-run centers often limit membership to residents, so call before you go.

faq.q: How much does lunch cost at a Bergen County senior center?
faq.a: Lunch is free for people 60 and older and their spouses, with a suggested donation of $1.25. Reserve by 11:30 a.m. the day before.

faq.q: How do I find a senior center near my mom in Bergen County?
faq.a: Start with the tables on this page, then call the Division of Senior Services at 201-336-7400. Staff can tell you the closest center and whether Community Transportation can pick her up.

faq.q: Can someone who no longer drives get a ride to the center?
faq.a: Yes. Bergen County Community Transportation provides rides to and from all the county centers. Call 201-368-5955 and press 1 for dispatch.

faq.q: What if my parent has dementia?
faq.a: A busy center may not be the right fit. Call the county at 201-336-7400 to ask about adult day programs, which offer more supervision.

body:
Essex County does senior centers a little differently from its neighbors. The county runs a lunch program called Cafe in the Parks, with hot meals served inside county parks. Almost everything else, from chair yoga to bingo to trips, is run by your own town. Newark alone has five senior centers.

This guide pulls it together: what centers offer, a table of the places we confirmed on official pages, how lunch and rides work, and what to do if your town has no center. It is for older adults and for the family members who often make the first call.

What do Essex County senior centers offer, and who can go?

Each town sets its own rules, so age limits and fees vary. Irvington and East Orange list their centers for residents 60 and older. North Caldwell's group is for residents 62 and up. Maplewood's programs start at 55, and Belleville residents 50 and older can register for the Senior Pass that opens its center. Most town programs are free or low cost, and many ask you to register with the recreation or senior services office first.

What you find inside depends on the town. Nutley's Senior Club meets Wednesday afternoons from September to June. Bloomfield's program at the Oakeside Cultural Center meets Monday and Wednesday afternoons with lunch, chair yoga, crafts and bingo, and no registration is needed. Newark's five centers are open Tuesday to Friday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., and Saturday, 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., with hot meals, fitness classes and cultural celebrations. The Grover Cleveland Senior Center in Caldwell is open to anyone 60 and over.

In Essex, the best first call is usually your own town hall, then the county.

The county's Cafe in the Parks sites serve lunch to anyone 60 and older, Monday to Friday, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. The provider that runs them countywide, Chr-ill Care, answers questions about all seven.

How does the county lunch program work?

The Essex County Division of Senior Services runs group meals through three provider agencies. All sites are open to people 60 and older.

  • Chr-ill Care serves the Cafe in the Parks sites countywide: 973-744-8103.
  • FOCUS serves the City of Newark with Hispanic meals: 973-624-2528.
  • Jewish Community Center of MetroWest serves kosher meals countywide: 973-530-3414.

Call the provider before your first visit to ask about reservations and the menu. The county's nutrition coordinator is at 973-395-8391. Some town centers, including Newark's and Bloomfield's, serve their own lunch, so ask your town too.

For someone who cannot get out, the same three agencies deliver meals at home to people 60 and older who cannot prepare their own. Our Meals on Wheels guide explains how to apply.

How can you get to a center without driving?

Essex County Special Transportation, run for the county by Transdev, carries older and disabled adults to non-emergency medical and therapy appointments. The county also lists mall shopping, group trips and other destinations. Book at least two business days ahead at 973-737-7200. Drivers give arm assistance but do not help with stairs, and the vans are wheelchair equipped.

Many towns run their own senior buses, often free. Millburn's bus, for example, takes residents 62 and older to activities, shopping and the library on set days. Ask your town's senior office. Essex is also one of the easier counties to get around by NJ Transit, and our guide to reduced fares explains the discount for riders 62 and over.

In our October 2026 conversations with North Jersey instructors, families and care professionals, many people said older adults give up activities they love only because they can no longer get there. A regular ride to the center can be the difference. See also when a parent stops driving.

What if your town has no senior center?

  • Use a neighbor's center. The Grover Cleveland Senior Center in Caldwell is open to anyone 60 and over, which helps if you live in Essex Fells or West Caldwell. Caldwell, West Caldwell and Roseland residents can also ride the shared senior bus (973-226-5108, call between 8:15 and 8:45 a.m. on the day you want to travel).
  • Eat at a Cafe in the Parks site. Any Essex County resident 60 or older can join.
  • Call the county. The Essex County ADRC (Aging and Disability Resource Connection) at 973-395-8375 or 1-877-222-3737 can point you to programs near you.
  • Look at the library. Roseland's senior group meets at its library, and many libraries host talks and clubs. Our staying connected guide has more ideas.

What helps on a first visit?

  1. Call the town office first. Ask about registration, what to bring and which day is busiest.
  2. Bring ID and proof of address. Many Essex towns limit programs to residents.
  3. Start with something specific. A chair yoga class or a lunch is easier than an open afternoon. Our chair yoga guide explains what a class is like.
  4. Go along once. Adult children can come to the first session and leave once their parent has a seat and a name tag.
  5. Give it a few weeks. A standing weekly class gives people something to look forward to and a reason to get dressed and out the door.

For families: if a parent needs more support than a center offers, ask the ADRC about adult day programs, or see care help near you.

faq.q: Does Essex County run its own senior centers?
faq.a: The county runs a lunch program, Cafe in the Parks, at seven county parks for people 60 and older. Most senior centers are run by towns, so check your town's senior services or recreation office too.

faq.q: Is there a kosher senior lunch in Essex County?
faq.a: Yes. The Jewish Community Center of MetroWest provides kosher meals countywide for the county's nutrition program. Call 973-530-3414.

faq.q: How do I get my dad to the senior center if he doesn't drive anymore?
faq.a: Ask his town about its senior bus first. Essex County Special Transportation (973-737-7200) mainly handles medical rides and some shopping and group trips, booked two business days ahead.

faq.q: What are the hours at Newark's senior centers?
faq.a: Newark lists Tuesday to Friday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., and Saturday, 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., closed Sunday and Monday. Call 973-733-6454 to find the nearest of the five centers.

faq.q: My town has no senior center. Where can I go?
faq.a: You can join a Cafe in the Parks lunch site anywhere in the county. The Grover Cleveland Senior Center in Caldwell is also open to anyone 60 and over. The ADRC at 973-395-8375 can suggest others.

title: Senior centers in Hudson County, NJ: locations, hours and programs
dek: Nearly every Hudson County town runs its own senior program, and free TRANSCEND vans can get you there. Here are the centers we confirmed, plus lunch, rides and first-visit tips.
keyFacts: Hudson County Division on Aging Services: 201-369-4313
Services are for residents 60 and older and their caregivers
TRANSCEND rides are free, weekdays 7:30 a.m. to 7 p.m.: 201-369-4320 ext. 4107
Most senior centers are run by towns, usually for their own residents
body:
In Hudson County, senior centers are close to home. The county is small and dense, and nearly every town runs its own senior program, often with a lunch room, a bingo schedule and a bus to the supermarket. The Hudson County Division on Aging Services funds and coordinates much of it, and the county's free TRANSCEND vans can bring older adults to nutrition sites.

This guide lists the centers and senior offices we confirmed on official town pages, explains lunch and rides, and gives some first-visit tips for older adults and the family members helping them.

What do Hudson County senior centers offer, and who can go?

The county's Division on Aging Services serves residents 60 and older and their caregivers. It works with town senior affairs offices on recreation, an annual senior luncheon, summer cruises and a senior art show. Its funded services include congregate meals, home-delivered meals, physical activity, education and socialization.

Day to day, the town is what matters. A few examples from town pages:

  • Jersey City runs the Joseph Connors and Maureen Collier senior centers, both with lunch, classes and bingo, through its Division of Senior Affairs.
  • Hoboken's Multi Service Center is open Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., with trips, art classes, bingo, yoga and help with benefits in English, Spanish and Italian.
  • North Bergen offers free tai chi, chair yoga, chair aerobics and chair Zumba, and free rides to the center for people on its pickup list.
  • Secaucus opens its center to residents 55 and over, with speakers, games, billiards, yoga and a gardening club.
  • Weehawken holds chair yoga, knitting and the Senior Citizen's Club at its Senior Nutrition Center, plus bingo in senior housing community rooms.
  • Kearny's Henrietta Benstead center is a friendship club run by older residents themselves, with a $10 yearly membership.
  • Harrison's Senior Center has daily activities for people 60 and older and a meal site serving lunch Monday to Friday.

Most programs are free or very low cost, but towns usually limit them to their own residents. Bring ID with your address when you sign up.

In a county this compact, the senior center is often a short walk or one bus ride away.

Where are the senior centers in Hudson County?

These are the centers and senior offices we confirmed on official town websites. Where a town lists a senior affairs office instead of a center, call the office for the current activity schedule.

Guttenberg and East Newark are not listed because we could not confirm a current program on an official page. Call the county at 201-369-4313 for help in those towns. More local details are on our Hudson County page.

How does the lunch program work?

Hudson County funds congregate meals for residents 60 and older under the Older Americans Act, and in practice you sign up through your town. Some examples: Harrison serves lunch at its senior center Monday to Friday and posts the weekly menu there every Monday morning. Weehawken runs meals from its Senior Nutrition Center (201-319-6060) and the Gregory Avenue Community Room. Jersey City's two centers both serve lunch.

Call your town senior office to ask about the lunch days, whether you need to reserve and what the suggested donation is. If your parent is homebound, ask the same office about home-delivered meals. Weehawken, for instance, signs people up at 201-319-6060. Our Meals on Wheels guide covers the basics.

How can you get to a center without driving?

TRANSCEND, the Hudson County Office of Transportation Services, gives free, curb to curb rides to residents 60 and older, adults 18 and older with disabilities, and veterans. Nutrition sites are on its list of destinations, along with medical visits, shopping and bus and rail connections. It runs Monday to Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 7 p.m., mostly within Hudson County with limited service to Essex and Bergen. Rides are shared and every van is wheelchair accessible. Call 201-369-4320 ext. 4107.

Town buses fill in the gaps. Weehawken offers free door to door supermarket trips and free medical rides. Bayonne residents can ride the free BEOF senior bus, and West New York lists medical transportation at 201-295-4540. Hudson is also well served by NJ Transit buses and the light rail. See our guide to reduced fares for riders 62 and over.

What if your town has no senior center?

  • Call your town senior affairs office anyway. Bayonne and Union City, for example, run their programs through an office rather than a single center.
  • Call the county. The Hudson County Division on Aging Services is at 201-369-4313, or call the statewide ADRC (Aging and Disability Resource Connection) at 1-877-222-3737.
  • Try the library or senior housing. Many Hudson programs run in library rooms and senior building community rooms. Our staying connected guide has more ideas.

What helps on a first visit?

  1. Call and ask for a calendar. Many Hudson towns post monthly senior calendars, some in English and Spanish.
  2. Bring ID with your address. Town programs usually check residency. Jersey City also issues Senior Care photo ID cards.
  3. Book a ride early. If you need TRANSCEND, call well before the day you want to go.
  4. Pick a familiar activity. Bingo, a chair exercise class or a birthday party lunch is an easy first step.
  5. Come along, then step back. Adult children can go to the first visit and leave once a parent is settled.

In our October 2026 conversations with North Jersey instructors, families and care professionals, people said seeing others and having something to look forward to every week mattered as much as any class. If your parent is wary of new places, a regular lunch day is a gentle start. For more support at home, see when a parent lives alone or care help near you.

faq.a: Most town programs are free or very low cost, and lunch is usually by suggested donation. Some clubs charge small dues, like Kearny's $10 a year. Call your town to confirm.

faq.a: Yes, if she is a Hudson County resident 60 or older. TRANSCEND lists nutrition sites among its destinations and charges no fees. Call 201-369-4320 ext. 4107 to book.

faq.q: Who runs senior centers in Hudson County, the county or the towns?
faq.a: Mostly the towns. The county Division on Aging Services funds and coordinates services, including meals, while town senior offices run the centers and activities.

faq.q: Is there a senior lunch in Weehawken?
faq.a: Yes. Weehawken runs its senior nutrition program from the Senior Nutrition Center at 201 Highwood Avenue and the Gregory Avenue Community Room. Call 201-319-6060.

faq.a: Call the town hall and ask for the senior affairs office, or call the county Division on Aging Services at 201-369-4313.

body:
Morris County has two layers of senior centers. The county's Nutrition Program runs thirteen Mid-Day Friendship Centers, where anyone 60 or older can have a free lunch and join activities. Many towns also run their own senior centers or clubs, from Florham Park's yellow building behind the municipal complex to the Senior Center of the Chathams.

This guide lists both, explains how to reserve lunch and get a ride through MAPS, and offers tips for a first visit, for older adults and for the family members who are often the ones searching.

What do Morris County senior centers offer, and who can go?

The county's Mid-Day Friendship Centers are open from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on their scheduled days. Each serves a midday meal and offers recreational, social and educational activities. The meal is free, and a $2 donation per meal is recommended.

Town centers set their own hours and rules. Morristown's center is open weekdays, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., for Town of Morristown residents, with exercise classes, day trips, the Sixty-Plus Club and help with benefits. Florham Park's center is open weekdays, 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The Senior Center of the Chathams is open weekdays, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., and Madison residents can use it through a shared service agreement. Several towns run clubs with small dues: East Hanover's and Hanover Township's senior clubs are for residents 60 and over at $10 a year, and the Township of Morris Senior Club is also $10 a year.

A free lunch, a table of familiar faces and a reason to leave the house on Tuesday: that is what a Friendship Center offers.

How do you reserve lunch?

  1. Find the nearest site. Use the table above. Note the days, since some sites serve only once or twice a week.
  2. Call that site's number. Ask to register for congregate dining. Mount Olive and Roxbury residents get the lunch phone listed above, which differs from the town's main senior line.
  3. Show up between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. The meal is free. A $2 donation is recommended but not required.

Questions about the program go to the county Nutrition Program at 973-285-6856. If your parent cannot get out to eat, ask the same office about home-delivered meals, or read our Meals on Wheels guide.

How can you get to a center without driving?

MAPS, the Morris Area Paratransit System, is a curb to curb shared ride service for Morris County residents who are 60 or older, veterans, people with disabilities, or people who live in rural parts of the county. You apply first, online, by email, fax or mail, with proof of age such as a driver's license or passport. The county says it contacts online applicants within one business day.

The suggested donation for general riders is $1 per round trip. MAPS covers medical trips, social services and grocery shopping. Call 973-829-8103 or 888-282-6277 to ask whether it can take your parent to a lunch site or senior center near them.

Some towns add their own rides. Morristown's center offers medical transportation and grocery help for residents. Ask your town. In our October 2026 conversations with North Jersey instructors, families and care professionals, many said older adults stop doing what they love only because they can no longer get there. Our guide on when a parent stops driving covers more options.

What if your town has no senior center?

  • Use a county lunch site. The Friendship Centers are open to Morris County residents 60 and older from any town.
  • Look for a shared center. Madison and the Chathams share one. Neighboring towns sometimes welcome guests, so ask.
  • Call the county. The Morris County ADRC (Aging and Disability Resource Connection) helpline is 973-285-6848, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., or call 1-877-222-3737.
  • Try the library. Morris libraries host talks, clubs and tech help. See staying connected.

What helps on a first visit?

  1. Call ahead. Reserve lunch and ask what activity is planned that day.
  2. Bring proof of age and address. Clubs and town centers usually register residents.
  3. Choose a day with something you like. Cards, a speaker or chair yoga. Our mahjong and bridge guide may spark an idea.
  4. Go together once. An adult child or friend can make the first lunch less awkward.
  5. Make it a habit. The same day each week becomes something to look forward to.

For families: if your parent needs more support than a center gives, ask the ADRC about adult day programs or see care help near you.

title: Senior centers in Passaic County, NJ: locations, hours and programs
dek: Passaic County runs seven senior nutrition centers with a hot weekday lunch for anyone 60 or older, and towns add their own clubs and classes. Here is where to go and how to get there.

body:
Passaic County runs seven senior nutrition centers, from the city of Passaic up to West Milford, where anyone 60 or older can have a hot weekday lunch and join parties, trips and talks. Many towns add their own senior offices, clubs and classes on top of that.

This guide lists the county centers and the town programs we confirmed on official pages, explains how meals and rides work, and gives tips for a first visit for older adults and the family members helping them.

What do Passaic County senior centers offer, and who can go?

The county's Division of Nutrition Services runs the seven centers. Each serves one hot meal Monday to Friday in a social setting and runs activities such as parties, trips and lectures. The county brochure lists hours of 8:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. at every center. The only requirement is age: you must be 60 or older, or the spouse of someone who is. Contributions are voluntary and confidential, and services do not depend on whether you give.

Town programs vary. Paterson's Division of Senior Services at Riverside Vets is open weekdays, 7:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., with chair exercise, Zumba, bingo, karaoke, crafts and trips. Wayne's age-friendly program offers health talks, screenings and low-cost exercise classes, with registration ahead of time. Ringwood's club is for residents 60 and older, and Woodland Park's Seniors Club welcomes anyone 50 or older. Clifton's Office of Senior Citizen and Disabled Services helps with forms, heating and cooling grants and Medicare counseling.

The county centers ask only one thing: that you are 60 or older, or married to someone who is.

How does the lunch program work?

Call the center you want to visit and ask how to sign up and whether to reserve a meal in advance. Lunch is offered Monday to Friday. The county posts a monthly menu on its Nutrition Services page.

For someone who cannot get to a center, Passaic County Meals on Wheels delivers one hot meal a day, Monday to Friday, with weekend service if needed. Applicants must live in Passaic County, be 60 or older (or live with a recipient who is), be homebound and be at high nutritional risk. Applications are taken by phone at 973-569-4099. Our Meals on Wheels guide explains what to expect from the home visit.

How can you get to a center without driving?

The Passaic County Paratransit Program gives non-emergency rides to older and disabled residents, including to county-run nutrition and adult day sites, medical appointments and shopping. Lift vans carry people who use wheelchairs. Which number you call depends on where you live:

  • Clifton residents: 973-470-2235
  • City of Passaic residents: 973-365-5754
  • Everyone else: 973-305-5756

Have your name, address, phone, date of birth, an emergency contact, any mobility device, the trip date, the destination's name, address and phone, and your return time ready. Some towns also run their own buses. Wayne's senior bus, for example, runs set routes to local sites for Wayne older adults (973-694-1800 ext. 3260).

In our October 2026 conversations with North Jersey instructors, families and care professionals, people said many older adults give up activities only because they can no longer get there. If your parent recently stopped driving, see our guide on when a parent stops driving.

What if your town has no senior center?

  • Use a county center. They are open to anyone 60 or older, so you can pick the one closest to you even if it is in another town.
  • Ask about clubs. Pompton Lakes, Little Falls, Totowa and Woodland Park all have senior clubs that meet weekly or twice a month.
  • Call the county. The Passaic County Department of Senior Services, Disability and Veterans' Affairs is at 973-569-4060, or call the ADRC (Aging and Disability Resource Connection) at 1-877-222-3737.
  • Check the library. Libraries often host free programs. See staying connected.

What helps on a first visit?

  1. Call the center first. Ask about the meal, the day's activity and the best time to arrive.
  2. Bring ID. Proof of age helps for the county centers, and town clubs often ask for proof of residency.
  3. Book the ride early. Paratransit fills up, so call as soon as you know the day.
  4. Plan for a short morning. County centers close at 1 p.m., so lunch is the heart of the day.
  5. Go with your parent once. Then let them make it their own. A weekly lunch date gives them something to look forward to.

For families: if a center is not enough support, ask the county about social adult day care, or see care help near you.

faq.a: The county lists 8:30 a.m. to 1 p.m., Monday to Friday, at all seven nutrition centers. Town programs keep their own hours.

faq.a: Call Passaic County Paratransit. Clifton residents call 973-470-2235, City of Passaic residents call 973-365-5754, and everyone else calls 973-305-5756.

How does the Senior Cafe lunch program work?

The Union County Division on Aging runs congregate lunches through the local Meals on Wheels provider. The county says there are more than 20 nutrition sites, including two kosher sites. Anyone 60 or older, or married to someone 60 or older, can take part. There are no income rules. The suggested donation is $1.75 per meal, it is confidential, and no one is turned away for not paying.

You must reserve at least two days ahead by calling the site you want to visit. Some sites ask for more notice. Kenilworth, for example, takes lunch reservations a week ahead, by Wednesday for the following week. Several town centers in the table, including Union, Hillside, Kenilworth, Linden's Gregorio Center, Plainfield, Roselle Park's Casano Center and Elizabeth's centers, have been Senior Cafe sites. To find the site nearest you and its current days, call the Division on Aging at 908-527-4870 or toll free at 1-888-280-8226.

title: Senior centers in Sussex County, NJ: locations, hours and programs
dek: Sussex County serves senior lunches in Franklin, Vernon and Hopatcong, and towns like Sparta, Newton and Byram run clubs. Here is where to go and how Skylands Ride can get you there.

body:
Sussex County is New Jersey's rural corner, and its senior centers reflect that. There are fewer of them, the drives are longer, and the county's Skylands Ride vans matter a great deal. The Sussex County Division of Senior Services runs three senior lunch sites, in Franklin, Vernon and Hopatcong, and several towns add clubs and programs of their own.

This guide lists what we confirmed on official county and town pages, explains how lunch and rides work, and offers tips for a first visit, written for older adults and for the family members who often make the call.

What do Sussex County senior centers offer, and who can go?

The county's Congregate Nutrition Program is for people 60 and older. At each site you can have a nutritious midday meal, socialize and join activities. The county lists exercise, yoga, crafts, Wii games and tournaments, theme parties, guest speakers and health courses, and activities vary by site. The program is funded under the Older Americans Act.

For a son or daughter who lives an hour away, a lunch site is also a quiet safety net. It means your parent sees familiar faces during the week, and staff who know them by name. In a county where neighbors can be far apart, that regular contact counts for a lot.

Town programs fill in around the county sites:

  • Sparta's Recreation Department runs a needle arts group and mahjong on Fridays at Knoll Heights Village, a monthly bingo, and a Thursday luncheon with a speaker on chosen dates. Its office is on the lower level of the library.
  • Newton's Prime Time Seniors is open to Sussex County residents 55 and older. Meetings are the first and third Wednesday, starting at 12:30 p.m. Membership is easy: just show up and sign up.
  • Byram's Senior Citizens Club meets the second and fourth Thursday at 1 p.m. at the township fire house on Route 206, for residents 55 and older, with lunches and bus trips through the year.
In a county this rural, a ride is part of the plan. Book Skylands Ride when you pick the day.

How does the county lunch program work?

Call the site you want to visit to ask which days it serves lunch and how to reserve a meal. The program is open to anyone 60 or older. Lunch is the center of the day, with activities around it.

If your parent cannot get out, ask the Division of Senior Services about home-delivered meals. Our Meals on Wheels guide covers how those programs usually work.

How can you get to a center without driving?

Skylands Ride, the county's transit service, runs several programs. Call 973-579-0480 for all of them.

  • Assisted Transportation serves residents 60 and older who need more help, weekdays, for medical trips, shopping and vital errands. Ask for the Assisted Transportation Program.
  • Hardyston and Vernon Paratransit serves residents 60 and older and people with disabilities on weekdays. Destinations include the senior center and nutrition site, shopping and medical appointments.
  • Employment Transportation is a lift-equipped, demand-response bus open to the general public, including older adults, weekdays from 5:30 a.m. to 6 p.m.
  • Veterans with at least 90 days of active service can ride on Thursdays to VA facilities in East Orange, Morristown and Lyons.

The county's lunch page points anyone who needs a ride to Skylands Ride at the same number. You can email a request, but it is not confirmed until the office replies with a pickup time.

Towns help too. Sparta's free Senior Surrey takes Sparta residents over 60 to Newton on Monday, Wednesday and Friday mornings and to local errands in the afternoons. Call 973-729-8542 on weekdays, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Newton also runs a senior shuttle; ask Newton Recreation at 973-383-3521 ext. 231.

In our October 2026 conversations with North Jersey instructors, families and care professionals, people told us many older adults give up what they love only because they can no longer get there. That is especially true in rural Sussex. See also when a parent stops driving.

What if your town has no senior center?

  • Use a county lunch site. Franklin, Vernon and Hopatcong serve older adults from around the county, and Skylands Ride can help you get there.
  • Join a regional club. Newton's Prime Time Seniors welcomes Sussex County residents 55 and older from any town.
  • Call the county. The Division of Senior Services is at 973-579-0555, or call the statewide ADRC (Aging and Disability Resource Connection) at 1-877-222-3737. Its free monthly Senior Times newsletter lists programs countywide.
  • Check the library. Sussex libraries host talks and clubs. See staying connected.

What helps on a first visit?

  1. Call the site and Skylands Ride the same day. Line up the lunch and the ride together.
  2. Bring ID. Proof of age and address makes signing up easier.
  3. Check the weather. Rural roads in winter can cancel plans. Ask how the site announces closings. Our winter guide has more tips.
  4. Go together once. A son or daughter can drive the first time and meet the staff.
  5. Pick a standing day. Something to look forward to every week is the whole point.

For families: if your parent lives alone far from town, our guide to a parent living alone and care help near you can help you plan.

body:
Middlesex County has more senior centers than most New Jersey counties. Nearly every large town runs one, and Woodbridge alone has six. That is good news if your mom or dad lives here. It means a class, a card game or a hot lunch is often a short drive or bus ride away.

This guide lists every center on the county's official list, explains who can use them and what they cost, and covers the county lunch program and rides. It is written for older adults and for the adult children who often make the first phone call.

What do senior centers in Middlesex County offer?

Most centers here are run by the town, often together with a local Office on Aging. Programs vary, but a typical week includes exercise classes, cards and games, crafts, lectures, health screenings, trips and holiday parties. Many centers also have staff who help with forms for programs like PAAD, Senior Freeze and Lifeline.

The real value is routine. Families tell us the same things matter most: staying safe at home, staying sharp, seeing people and having something to look forward to every week. A standing Tuesday exercise class and a Thursday lunch can do all four.

Who can use them, and what do they cost?

Most centers serve residents 60 and older, but each town sets its own rules. Some limit membership to town residents. Others welcome neighbors from nearby towns for some programs. Expect to fill out a short registration form and show proof of age and address.

Joining is usually free or close to it. Some classes and trips carry a fee. The county lunch program asks for a donation instead of a price, covered below. When in doubt, call the center and ask three questions: Do I have to live in town? Is there a membership fee? Which programs cost extra?
