How can my parent get to a senior center?

Middlesex County RIDE offers shared rides by reservation for residents 60 and older and adults 18 and up with disabilities. Call 1-800-221-3520 to book, and ask about the suggested fare when you call. RIDE also runs fixed shuttle routes with a suggested fare of 50 cents for older adults and riders with disabilities. RIDE started a new scheduling system on October 5, 2026, so expect some adjustments.

The county says transportation can be arranged to its meal sites. Several towns also run their own senior buses, so ask the center directly.

In our October 2026 conversations with families and care professionals, many said older adults stop going out only because they can no longer get there.

A ride can be the difference. If your parent has just given up the car keys, read when a parent stops driving and NJ Transit reduced fares.

What if my town has no senior center?

Start with the county Office of Aging and Disabled Services at 732-745-3295 or the statewide Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737. Ask whether a nearby center accepts residents from your town. Some do, especially for lunch, since the meal program is county-wide.

Other good options are the public library (book clubs, tech help, talks), parks and recreation programs, and houses of worship. See staying connected in New Jersey for more. For residents near the county line, Somerset County's centers and Monmouth County's centers are also listed on this site, though most limit membership to their own residents.

What should we know before the first visit?

The first visit is the hardest one. After that, most people find a table, a class or a group they like. A little planning helps, whether you are going yourself or nudging a parent to try it.

  1. Call ahead. Ask about membership, what ID to bring, which days are busiest and whether lunch needs a reservation. Ask for the monthly calendar or newsletter.
  2. Pick one thing to try. A chair exercise class, a card game or a lecture gives a reason to walk in and something to talk about. Lunch alone in a new room can feel awkward. Lunch after a class feels natural.
  3. Bring paperwork. Most centers ask for proof of age and address, and a short registration form. Have an emergency contact name and number ready.
  4. Go together the first time. If you are the adult child, sit in on the first class or stay for lunch. Then step back. Many people warm up faster when family is not hovering.
  5. Give it three visits. One visit is not a fair test. Regulars learn names quickly, and staff often introduce newcomers.

If your parent is resisting, avoid calling it a senior center at first. Talk about the class, the card game or the lunch. Many people in their 70s do not think of themselves as seniors, and that is fine. For more ideas on the first talk, see how to start the conversation.

A note on trust and safety

Senior centers are public places, and staff will not ask for bank or Medicare numbers to join a bingo game. Be careful with anyone at an event who pushes insurance plans, investments or home repair deals. If something feels off, ask the center staff. Our New Jersey scams guide lists the tricks that come up most.

For county services in one place, see our Middlesex County page.

body:
Monmouth County runs from Bayshore towns like Keyport and Highlands down to the beaches of Long Branch and Asbury Park, with farm country and suburbs inland. Senior centers here are mostly run by towns, and the county keeps an official list of them.

Below you will find that list with addresses and phone numbers, along with who can join, where lunch is served, and how to get a ride. If you are helping a parent from out of town, this is a good page to bookmark.

What do Monmouth County senior centers offer?

Expect a monthly calendar of exercise classes, cards and games, crafts, lectures, health screenings, day trips and parties. Some centers double as a town's human services office, so staff can help with applications and point you to local help. A few also serve lunch through the county's nutrition program.

For many people the draw is simpler than any single class. It is a reason to get dressed and out the door, a familiar face at the front desk and a group that notices when you miss a week. Those small things help people stay steady on their feet, stay sharp and avoid the isolation that often follows retirement, a move or the loss of a spouse.

Who can use them, and what do they cost?

Because each town runs its own center, the rules differ. Most serve residents 60 and older, and many ask you to register with proof of age and address. Some towns welcome residents of neighboring towns for certain programs. Joining is usually free, with small fees for some classes and trips.

The Monmouth County Division on Aging, Disabilities and Veterans Services serves residents 60 and older and their caregivers. Call 732-431-7450 if you are not sure where to start.

How can my parent get to a senior center?

You must book four days ahead. Rides run Monday through Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., and priority goes to medical trips and food shopping, so a senior center trip may depend on space. Call 732-431-6480.

This guide explains how the centers work, who can use them, and how to get there. It is written for older adults and for family members who may be arranging things from a distance.

What do Warren County senior centers offer?

The county invites residents to its senior community centers for lunch, socializing and exercise or activities. Each center posts a monthly activity calendar on the county website, so you can see what is coming before you go.

The Division also runs virtual classes for residents 60 and older who would rather stay home: meditation, chair yoga and tai chi. You register in advance, sign a release form, and the suggested donation is $2 per class. Donations are voluntary. Call 908-475-6591 to sign up. To register for the senior meal program, call the Division at 908-475-6591. Home-delivered meals are also available for homebound older adults who meet program guidelines, and the county says it is accepting new participants. See our Meals on Wheels guide to understand how home delivery works.

How can my parent get to a senior center?

Warren County Transportation offers curb-to-curb rides for residents over 60 and residents with disabilities, as well as honorably discharged veterans and residents of rural areas. The suggested fare is $1 per trip. To ride to a nutrition site, your parent must first register with the Division of Aging and Disability Services at 908-475-6591.

For demand response trips, call Easton Coach at 908-454-4044 (option 2) or 1-866-594-4044 at least three business days ahead. Rides cover all of Warren County and five miles beyond. Two public shuttles also link Phillipsburg, Washington and Hackettstown on weekdays, with Saturday service between Phillipsburg and Washington. Drivers can make short detours off the route when conditions allow if you ask.

For registered older adults, the county also runs Senior Saturday Shopping on the second and fourth Saturday of the month. Call Senior Services at 908-475-6591 to sign up, with three business days' notice. A shopping trip with familiar faces can be its own small social outing, and it often leads to the lunch table at the center.

Getting there is half the battle in a county this size.

What if none of the centers is close?

Try the virtual classes, home-delivered meals, or programs at the Warren County Library and local churches. Call the Division at 908-475-6591 or the statewide ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 for help. Our parent living alone guide covers check-in calls and other ways to stay in touch from a distance.

Near the Hunterdon line? See senior centers in Hunterdon County, though membership there is for Hunterdon residents.

The first visit is the hardest one. After that, most people find a table, a class or a group they like. A little planning helps, whether you are going yourself or nudging a parent to try it.

  1. Call ahead. Ask about membership, what ID to bring, which days are busiest and whether lunch needs a reservation. Ask for the monthly calendar or newsletter.
  2. Pick one thing to try. A chair exercise class, a card game or a lecture gives a reason to walk in and something to talk about. Lunch alone in a new room can feel awkward. Lunch after a class feels natural.
  3. Bring paperwork. Most centers ask for proof of age and address, and a short registration form. Have an emergency contact name and number ready.
  4. Go together the first time. If you are the adult child, sit in on the first class or stay for lunch. Then step back. Many people warm up faster when family is not hovering.
  5. Give it three visits. One visit is not a fair test. Regulars learn names quickly, and staff often introduce newcomers.

Senior centers are public places, and staff will not ask for bank or Medicare numbers to join a bingo game. Be careful with anyone at an event who pushes insurance plans, investments or home repair deals. If something feels off, ask the center staff. Our New Jersey scams guide lists the tricks that come up most.

For more county resources, see our Warren County page.

title: Senior centers in Burlington County, NJ: locations, hours and programs
dek: Where to find senior centers and lunch clubs in Burlington County, who can go, what lunch costs and how to get a ride there with Sen-Han Transit.
keyFacts: The county Golden Years Luncheon Club serves people 60+ at four sites: Beverly, Bordentown, Moorestown and Mount Holly.
Suggested lunch donation is $2.00, and no one is refused for being unable to pay.
Sen-Han Transit gives rides to residents 60+ and drives to the Beverly, Bordentown and Moorestown clubs. Call 877-603-5111.

body:
Burlington County is the biggest county in New Jersey by land, which makes "just pop over to the senior center" harder than it sounds. A lunch club in Beverly is a long way from a farmhouse in Tabernacle. The good news is that the county runs four lunch clubs, many towns run their own centers, and a county funded van service can get your parent there.

This guide lists the centers we could confirm on official county and town websites, explains how the county lunch works, and covers rides, first visits and what to do if your town has nothing nearby. For other county services, see our Burlington County page.

What do senior centers offer, and who can go?

A senior center is a drop in place for older adults to eat, move, learn and see people. A typical week might include a hot lunch, chair exercise or line dancing, cards and mahjong, bingo, crafts, a health talk and a blood pressure check. Many centers also run day trips and help with paperwork like Medicare questions or property tax relief forms.

That mix matters more than it sounds. Regular company and regular movement help people stay steady on their feet and sharp in conversation. See our fall prevention guide and staying connected for why.

Age rules, cost and residency

The county's lunch program, called the Golden Years Luncheon Club, is for people 60 and older. The county asks for a $2.00 donation per meal, but nobody is refused a meal for being unable to give. The clubs do not accept food stamps.

Town run centers set their own rules. Willingboro's Reva Foster Senior Center offers membership to eligible residents 55 and older. Mount Laurel lets residents 55 and older use its Community Center rooms on weekdays. Medford's Cranberry Hall Senior Center is run for Medford older adults with help from volunteers. Some classes and trips at any center carry a small fee or need advance sign up.

Where are the senior centers in Burlington County?

The first four rows are the county lunch clubs. The rest are municipal centers. Hours and programs change, so call before your first visit.

For Willingboro, press 6 for the Kennedy Center and then 2 for the senior center. Evesham's senior programs are run from the Gibson House office, and you can register for classes online or by phone. Mount Laurel residents can call Parks and Recreation at 856-234-0001, ext. 1241, about senior classes at the Community Center.

Other towns run senior clubs or programs too. If yours is not listed, call your municipal building or the county Office on Aging, which publishes a Directory of Services for older adults in Burlington County.

How does the county lunch program work?

Each Golden Years Luncheon Club serves lunch with activities around it: fitness, educational talks, board and card games and theme parties. Days differ by site:

  • Beverly: Monday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, 9 a.m. to 1 p.m.
  • Bordentown: Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday, 9 a.m. to 1 p.m.
  • Moorestown: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday, 9 a.m. to 1 p.m.
  • Mount Holly: Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m.

The county does not post a reservation rule online, so call the site you want a day or two ahead. Ask whether you need to sign up for lunch, what the menu is and when people usually arrive. For general questions, call the Burlington County Office on Aging at 609-265-5069. If getting out is not realistic, the county Meals on Wheels line is 609-702-7053.

Can my parent get a ride to the center?

Yes, in many cases. Sen-Han Transit, run by the nonprofit Senior Citizens United Community Services, provides rides for Burlington County residents 60 and older and for riders certified as disabled.

  • Lunch club rides. Sen-Han currently drives riders to three of the county lunch clubs: Beverly, Bordentown and Moorestown. Call the club or the Office on Aging to get on the list.
  • Personal business rides. These can be booked three days ahead for places within five miles of home. Call 877-603-5111, weekdays 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.
  • Medical rides. Book two days to two weeks ahead at the same number.
  • Weekly shopping trips. Sen-Han runs shopping service in 38 municipalities. Reserve the working day before at 856-255-5348.

Some towns run their own senior buses too. Evesham's senior services division manages a senior transit program, so ask your town hall first. If your parent has recently stopped driving, our guide to when a parent stops driving walks through the other options, including NJ Transit reduced fares on the River LINE.

What if your town has no senior center?

Plenty of towns in Burlington County do not run their own center. You still have options, and most are close by.

  • Use a neighboring center. County lunch sites are meant for county residents age 60 and older, not only people from the host town. Town run centers set their own rules, and some welcome non residents. Call and ask before you go.
  • Ask your town hall about a senior club. Many towns have a senior citizens club that meets once or twice a month in a firehouse, church hall or municipal building, with lunches, trips and speakers.
  • Try the library. Public libraries run book groups, tech help, lectures and crafts, usually free. See our guide to learning something new and free tech help.
  • Call the county. The Burlington County Office on Aging at 609-265-5069 knows every lunch site and club in the county and can tell you which ones have transportation from your street. The statewide Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) line, 1-877-222-3737, reaches the same office.

In Burlington County, remember the luncheon clubs are spread from the river towns to Mount Holly. If none is close, a Sen-Han shopping day or a library program can be the weekly outing instead.

If getting out is truly not possible right now, home delivered meals can fill the gap. See Meals on Wheels in New Jersey and activities for homebound older adults.

How do you make the first visit go well?

The first visit is the hardest one. Many older adults picture a room full of strangers who already know each other. Usually it is a friendly room where newcomers are welcome, but walking in alone still takes nerve. A little planning helps.

  1. Call first. Ask what day is busiest, what the lunch is that day, and whether there is a class or game that suits your interests. A specific reason to go is easier than "just showing up."
  2. Bring ID and a little cash. Some centers ask new members to fill out a short form with proof of age and address. Lunch donations and class fees are usually a few dollars.
  3. Go with someone the first time. A neighbor, a friend from church or a family member can ride along and stay for lunch. After one or two visits most people are comfortable on their own.
  4. Pick one activity and give it three weeks. Chair exercise, cards, a craft group or a talk. Regulars warm up to the people who keep coming back.
  5. Ask about the bulletin board. Senior centers are a good place to learn about tax help, Medicare counseling, flu clinics and trips you would never hear about otherwise.

A note for adult children

If you are the son or daughter doing the research, you are in good company. In our October 2026 conversations with North Jersey instructors, families and care professionals, the adult child (often a daughter) was frequently the one who found an activity and set it up. The parent then took it from there. Families told us what they hope for most: a parent who stays safe at home, stays sharp, sees people and has something to look forward to every week.

Some practical ways to help without taking over:

  • Frame it as one visit, not a commitment. "Let's try the Tuesday lunch once" is easier to say yes to.
  • Handle the logistics quietly. Book the first ride, put the center's number in your parent's phone and write the schedule on the fridge calendar.
  • Ask the staff what they see. Centers notice when a regular stops coming, seems confused or looks unwell. If you are worried, ask how they would reach you.
  • Keep the trust rules. Senior centers are public places with staff, which makes them a safe way to meet people. Still remind your parent never to share bank details or Medicare numbers with someone they just met, and never to pay for a "special offer" handed out in the parking lot. Our guide to scams in New Jersey lists the common ones.

faq.a: Sen-Han Transit gives rides to Burlington County residents 60 and older and currently serves the Beverly, Bordentown and Moorestown lunch clubs. Call 877-603-5111 on weekdays between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. Some towns also run their own senior buses, so ask your municipal building.

faq.a: Town run centers set their own rules. Willingboro's Reva Foster Senior Center offers membership to eligible residents 55 and older, and Mount Laurel's Community Center is for residents 55 and older. Call the center to ask.

faq.a: Call the Burlington County Office on Aging at 609-265-5069. Staff can point you to the nearest lunch club or senior club and tell you whether a ride is available. Libraries also run free programs.

faq.a: Yes. Burlington County runs Meals on Wheels for people 60 and older. Call 609-702-7053 to ask about eligibility.
